title: Hom from an ideal-power torsion module is unchanged under flat neighbourhood base change
statement: Let $\varphi:R\to S$ be a flat map of commutative rings [def-weil-pbc-flat-ring-map], let $I\subseteq R$ be a finitely generated ideal for which $R/I\to S/IS$ is an isomorphism, and let $K,N$ be $R$-modules with every element of $K$ annihilated by some power of $I$. Then scalar extension [def-weil-module-base-change] induces a bijection $\operatorname{Hom}_R(K,N)\to\operatorname{Hom}_S(K\otimes_RS,N\otimes_RS)$, $u\mapsto u\otimes_RS$. The bijection is natural in both modules.

source.place: More on Algebra, Lemma 05EC (lemma-neighbourhood-equivalence, line 24301), part (2), case of torsion source

proof.text: Let c:N -> S tensor_R N be n -> 1 tensor n and t:N[I^infinity] -> (S tensor_R N)[I^infinity] its restriction. The torsion-submodule comparison [lem-weil-pbc-torsion-submodule-flat-base-change-iso] makes t bijective, hence an R-linear equivalence e. Every k in K belongs to K[I^infinity] by the torsion hypothesis, including exponent zero (then k=0). Every R-linear map carries ideal-power torsion elements to ideal-power torsion elements.

proof.text: Injectivity: if f and h have equal scalar extensions, evaluation at 1 tensor k gives c(f(k))=c(h(k)) for every k. Both f(k) and h(k) lie in N[I^infinity], by linearity and torsion of k. Injectivity of t implies f(k)=h(k); extensionality gives f=h. In Lean this uses Ideal.primaryComponent_map_mem, subtype extensionality, and LinearMap.baseChange_tmul.

source.place: More on Algebra, Lemma 05EC (lemma-neighbourhood-equivalence), proof of part (2), torsion-source case, using part (1) directly on the restriction k -> g(1 tensor k)

proof.text: Surjectivity: given an S-linear g:S tensor_R K -> S tensor_R N, restrict it along k -> 1 tensor k to an R-linear d. Its image is in (S tensor_R N)[I^infinity], since k is torsion and d is R-linear. Corestrict d to this submodule and compose with e inverse and the inclusion N[I^infinity] -> N, obtaining an R-linear f:K -> N. The inverse-equivalence law gives c(f(k))=d(k)=g(1 tensor k). On every pure tensor s tensor k, the scalar extension of f equals s times c(f(k)), hence s times g(1 tensor k)=g(s tensor k). Tensor-product extensionality proves f.baseChange S=g. Thus the original scalar-extension map is bijective. Naturality remains LinearMap.baseChange_comp. This directly uses part (1) on the restricted map and does not require the separately stated torsion-module comparison or an invocation of the scalar-extension adjunction.
